newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MKT OUTLOOK -- T-bonds tread tight range.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MKT OUTLOOK -- T-bonds tread tight range.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities were expected to tread tight ranges on Friday, with market players refraining from taking major positions ahead of next week's barrage of top-tier data, analysts said.
If anything, analysts said, prices might get a brief jolt Friday if the durable goods data veer dramatically from Wall Street forecasts. The data are due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Don Fine, chief analyst at Chase Asset Management, saw durables up 1.7-2.0 percent but said if they are "very strong because of aircraft orders, the market will not overreact."
However, he said, "If the strength is away from the aircraft category, that will be a surprise and might unnerve a few people."

Economists polled by Reuters were calling for an average increase in orders of 1.4-percent, up from May's 0.7-percent decline. However, experts cautioned, the number is usually volatile and subject to sharp revisions.
Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp, said he expected durables to be a blowout, rising as much as 3.2 percent.

He attributed most of the gain to an increase in transportation orders, including a big bounce in motor vehicle shipments. But Liro said a confident Treasury market should be able to absorb a hearty number.
"The (Treasury) market is real strong," he said, adding the market may trade down if there is a lofty rise in durable goods orders, but buyers still would emerge on the downtrade.

Among data of lesser signifance, June existing home sales was set for release at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. A Reuters poll produced a consensus forecast that sales slipped to 4.19 million in June from 4.24 million in the previous month.
Market players were likely to shrug at the report, a few experts said, adding that the focus would soon shift toward a lengthy list of top-tier data next week.
"(Next week's) numbers should start to look a little bit better, which may limit any further gains by the market," said Fine.
Nevertheless, U.S. Treasury prices should stick to a narrow band.
"(Trading) will be relatively rangebound unless there are major surprises with the durable goods numbers," said Marilyn Schaja, an economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenerette Seucrities Corp.
Late Thursday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 102-18/32 bid, up 2/32, to yield 6.43 percent.
Ten-year notes were flat at 103-14/32 bid, yielding 6.15 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to yield 5.86 percent.
Federal funds rate is seen opening at 5.44 percent, slightly above the Fed's 5.50 percent target.
